PM has 'problem with telling the truth': Taylor
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says the prime minister has a "problem with telling the truth" as he ramps up pressure over $6m golf club grant.

Anthony Albanese initially said the funding for the Marrickville Golf Club was to fix sewerage issues. But after the infrastructure department confirmed the project didn't include any sewerage work, the prime minister told QT that defence "was not correct".
Speaking with 2SM, Taylor says Albanese has a problem with digging in.

"He didn't say 'I was not correct'. He said 'it was not correct' after pressuring on multiple occasions. This guy cannot admit that he got it wrong. And it just gives you huge insight into this prime minister and his character. His strategy is to dig in," he says.

"It's like when he changed his position on negative gearing and capital gains tax, like the furor over melons and the Japanese prime minister. It's like when he said he didn't fall off the stage and he clearly did. This prime minister has a problem with telling the truth".
Centrelink compliance regime resumes after system unlawfully cancelled payments
More than 50,000 welfare recipients could now get compensation after the government unlawfully stopped their payments, claiming they had failed to meet "mutual obligation" requirements.
That scheme, which was partially paused in July 2024, when concerns it may have been operating unlawfully first arose, has now restarted, with advocates warning the problems have not been fixed.
A Commonwealth Ombudsman investigation last year found 964 payment cancellations were not made in accordance with the law.

The Department of Employment and Workplace Relations (DEWR) said it had fixed the issues identified by the Commonwealth Ombudsman through IT system changes, system testing, improved participant communications and additional training for decision-makers.

But advocacy groups fear not enough has been done to fix the underlying issues, with questions set to be put to the government over the scale of the payment cancellations and what evidence it relied on before resuming the program.

Labor, Coalition brush off Shoebridge's $21-a-week tax cut proposal
We've had a bit of reaction this morning to Shoebridge's proposed tax plan.
Labor's Murray Watt said the Greens could make whatever promises they wanted, but they would not be in the frame to win government at the next election.

"The reality is that come the next election, we will either have a Labor government or a Coalition between the Liberals, Nationals and One Nation. They are the two options that are available to the Australian people, rather than a Greens party government," he told ABC's News Breakfast.
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson dismissed it as nothing but a "snake oil salesman pitch".

"They sell an easy snake oil salesman pitch, which is that if we just tax all these people over here, it's somehow going to end in us being able to [have] taxes over here," he told News24."David Shoebridge is very good at selling these myths to Australian people. I accept that, but it will only end up in higher taxes on every Australian."
"They sell an easy snake oil salesman pitch, which is that if we just tax all these people over here, it's somehow going to end in us being able to [have] taxes over here," he told News24.
"David Shoebridge is very good at selling these myths to Australian people. I accept that, but it will only end up in higher taxes on every Australian."
Shoebridge spruiks tax plan
Greens leader David Shoebridge has also been out and about this morning, spruiking his proposal for a $21-a-week tax cut paid for by gas and other resources.
The proposal would raise the tax-free threshold from $18,200 to $26,000 for all personal income taxpayers. It would also add the same amount to all income support payments.
Shoebridge tells ABC's News Breakfast it would be funded through a gas export tax, which he says Australians have been calling for.
"It's funded by getting a fair share on our resources. And I want to be clear that it more than pays for the tax relief that we're proposing for ordinary Australians," he says.
Shoebridge says it's a policy the government should consider.

One Nation cartoon team needs to explain how use of Bluey is satire: Wells
Communications Minister Anika Wells says the ABC is "well within its rights" to be concerned about One Nation cartoons that include a depiction of Bluey.
The public broadcaster's managing director, Hugh Marks, told Senate estimates the ABC would be taking further action over concerns it is a breach of intellectual property.
Wells says she supports the ABC's decision

"Bluey is one of Australia's biggest, most loved, most well-known exports. I think the ABC's well within its right to be concerned here. Given it's now looking at legal options, I shouldn't say any more, but I will say to you that Bluey has a lot more production value than One Nation's cartoons," she tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast.
Asked if the One Nation cartoon goes over the line of what satire is, Wells responds:
"Satire is one thing. Scrutiny is important," she says.
"I think that the people that are making this cartoon should explain why this errs on the side of satire and not something more."

O'Brien rejects claim Coalition is not engaging on digital duty of care
Liberal frontbencher Ted O'Brien has dismissed suggestions the opposition has refused to come to the table on the digital duty of care legislation.
"The government will not budge on this, which is why we have come to the point where we've just said they have to go back to the drawing board," he tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast.
Earlier, Communications Minister Anika Wells told the ABC the opposition was "refusing to participate" in negotiations.
O'Brien argues the Coalition has long been leaders in online safety, pointing to the fact it established the eSafety commissioner role.
But the opposition has concerns about the "extraordinary amount of power" the legislation hands that same commissioner, as well as the impact on small business.
Asked if the Coalition will eventually put up amendments when the bill heads to the Senate next month, O'Brien says he doesn't want to pre-empt the process.

Coalition 'refusing to participate' on digital duty of care: Wells
Communications Minister Anika Wells is up first on ABC's Radio National Breakfast discussing the digital duty of care bill.
The legislation would require online platforms to take reasonable steps to prevent a range of harms for children and limit adults' exposure to "serious" harms.
Wells is frustrated with the Coalition, which has resolved to oppose the legislation amid concerns of censorship.
"The opposition say they care about kids' safety online and I believe them. But parliament is where you prove it. So where are their amendments if they really care?" she says.

"There are Australian parents out there who elected Coalition MPs who expect their views to be part of this debate. And at the moment, they are not part of negotiations because the Coalition is refusing to participate."
Asked if Labor could consider supporting an amendment put by Sophie Scamps to establish a new industry-funded online ombudsman to resolve complaints, Wells did not directly say.
Wells says she's had good-faith negotiations with the Greens, but her door remains open to those who want to find ways to improve the bill.
The changing face of youth extremism
What drives a 12-year-old child from a loving, stable home to absorb violent online propaganda? That is a core challenge facing the Australian Federal Police amid new data tabled to Senate estimates.
The AFP analysed the histories of 55 radicalised youths and found online extremism is impacting children who show no history of family trauma or obvious vulnerability.

Every subject studied was male, aged between 12 and 17, and radicalised at least in part online. But while violent jihadism and white supremacy dominate, AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett warns that investigators are seeing a messy shift toward "mixed/hybrid ideologies, unclear/incoherent ideologies … and ideological fluidity."
While some of the radicalised youths faced trauma or lacked stability, Barrett notes that others came from completely secure family environments.

The AFP's deep dive into youth radicalisation did highlight a few common threads: 13 per cent were suspended in primary school, over one-third were kicked out of high school, and three in five had received mental health treatment.

With no single profile or predictable pathway, the AFP hopes this data will help police, educators and parents spot early warning signs, long before an online rabbit hole turns into real-world violence.

PM did not mislead parliament over golf club grant: Watt
Labor frontbencher Murray Watt has been deployed to defend the prime minister this morning over claims he misled the parliament.
He backed Anthony Albanese after he admitted it was "not correct" to have told the House of Reps that a $6 million grant to the Marrickville Golf Club in his electorate was for sewerage works.
"No, he didn't [mislead parliament]," Watt tells ABC's News Breakfast.

"The prime minister was correct in saying that the original announcement included that sewerage work to remove pollution going into the Cooks River. Obviously, the situation changed with the New South Wales government making a similar commitment."
Asked if there was a risk the government's response to my colleague Jake Evans's story was more damaging than the story itself, Watt disagreed.

Canavan accuses PM of lying over golf club grant
Nationals leader Matt Canavan has accused the prime minister of lying and misleading the parliament over a grant awarded to a golf club in his electorate.

"It's not just that the prime minister has a clear, loose relationship with the truth, it's that ... he takes so long to come clean every time ... it takes so long for him to come clean," he told Nine.

Anthony Albanese had previously told the House of Reps the $6 million grant for the Marrickville Golf Club was to fix sewerage issues. But he admitted that was "not correct" when asked in QT after the infrastructure department confirmed the project didn't include any sewerage work.
Labor frontbencher Amanda Rishworth, who was on the same panel, defended the PM.
She insisted the original proposal included sewerage works but the NSW government had stepped in.
Greens leader proposes $21-a-week tax cut in vow to 'replace Labor'
The Greens have called for a $21-a-week tax cut for all taxpayers and a welfare boost in the party's first major policy launch since its new leader vowed to "replace Labor".

David Shoebridge, whose first weeks in the role have been derailed by allegations against Greens senator Jordon-Steele John, will front the National Press Club on Wednesday to launch a tax policy to "turn the tide" on inequality.
The new proposal would raise the tax-free threshold from $18,200 to $26,000 for all personal income taxpayers, a tax cut of up to $1,092 a year or $21 a week.
It would also add the same amount to all income support payments, including the JobSeeker unemployment benefit, student and carer payments, and the Age Pension.
"No matter who you are, whether you're working, studying, looking for work or on a pension, you'll get more," he will say, according to an extract of a speech seen by the ABC.

The policy would cost the budget $22 billion each year, according to the independent Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO). Senator Shoebridge will propose the cost be offset by collecting "rivers of gold" from gas and mining companies.
US nuclear-powered submarine arrives in Australia
It's full steam ahead for AUKUS following the arrival of a US nuclear-powered attack submarine — USS Colorado — at HMAS Stirling yesterday for scheduled maintenance.
The visit serves as a trial run of sorts for the Submarine Rotational Force–West (SRF-West) plan.
What is that? Well, starting in late 2027, SRF-West will establish a permanent presence of up to five US and UK nuclear subs in Western Australia.

This will essentially boost the US and UK's military presence in the Indo-Pacific while giving Australian crews and technicians crucial hands-on experience with nuclear submarines before Australia acquires its own fleet in the 2030s.
Defence officials confirmed the Colorado will return as the inaugural vessel under that arrangement.

This week's maintenance work is basically an opportunity for Australian and allied technicians to show they're up to the task of servicing these high-tech submarines. But while Canberra points to the operation as proof of growing domestic capability, some sources I've spoken with remain concerned about Australia's ability to rapidly scale up local infrastructure and workforce numbers in time. It's a huge undertaking!

The Australian Submarine Agency chief Jonathan Mead said in a statement: "This is the fourth maintenance period since 2024. Each visit sees a significant growth in the number of Australians supporting maintenance on visiting boats, from local industry to Navy divers. It is genuinely exciting to see how far we've come as a country in such a short time."

Australia Post CEO reveals 'mind-blowing' bonus
Australia Post's chief executive Paul Graham has revealed he received a $1.2 million executive bonus on top of his $1.64 million base salary.

Fronting Senate estimates last night, Graham was asked by Liberal senator Sarah Henderson about his salary in relation to the company's performance results for the 2026 financial year, which included a pre-tax profit of $31.8 million.
An underlying loss of $107.6 million excluded profit from property sales of $139.4 million, according to the company.
The CEO told estimates "half" of his $1.2 million bonus was contingent on the company's "property strategy being executed".
"That's a mind-blowing amount of money," Henderson responded.
Graham will retire at the end of June 2027, and said the decision was made in consultation with his family.
"I'm 65 next month, I know I don't look it, and it's been a decision that has been coming for some time."

The Reserve Bank is also listed to appear. They'll join estimates around the same time the Australian Bureau of Statistics drops its latest inflation data.

Focus in the chamber is expected to stick with the government's digital duty of care legislation. But don't be surprised if the Coalition continues to pile on the pressure on the PM and the $6 million Marrickville Golf Club grant.
